newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Sweden still seeks minimal nickel in euro coins.
newsitem.headline: Sweden still seeks minimal nickel in euro coins.

text.p: Sweden will continue to try and convince other European Union members about the health benefits of minimising the nickel content of the bloc's planned euro coins, a senior finance ministry official said on Thursday.
But the issue was not likely to be discussed at this weekend's informal meeting of EU finance ministers in the Dutch coastal town of Noordwijk, state secretary Kari Lotsberg said.
"Probably, there won't be any discussions on this issue," she told Reuters.
Lotsberg said she believed there was increasing understanding in other capitals for the Swedish point of view.
Stockholm, which has not yet decided whether to join economic and monetary union (EMU), argues nickel can cause allergies and wants as little as possible of the metal in the new coins.

EU finance ministers postponed a decision on the sensitive issue at a meeting last month, and instructed the European Commission to come up with a compromise, which it has not yet done due to a lack of time, an EU official said.
This delay may turn out to be positive for the Swedish position as there would now be more time to test alternative metal combinations, Lotsberg said.
The euro coins are due to enter circulation in 2002 in countries participating in monetary union.

Finance Minister Erik Asbrink has made clear that Sweden could not accept an EU decision which meant that there would be a lot of nickel in the euro coins, saying it was an important question for his government.
"There is no doubt that there is a varying degree of awareness about the health problems...I am convinced that time is on our side," he said at last month's meeting.
Sweden had shown that there was a good alternative in the country's 10-crown coin which instead of nickel used a metal mix called "Nordic gold", consisting mainly of copper, he said.

The finance ministry refers to Swedish figures showing that 20 percent of young women in Europe are affected by nickel allergy, partly because of frequent exposure to the metal, for example by wearing earrings and other jewellery.

It strongly rejects suggestions that Stockholm's views reflect self-interest. The "Nordic gold" alloy was developed by a Swedish firm but is now produced by Finnish metal group Outokumpu and there is no patent on it, it says.
Apart from the nickel issue, last month's meeting also postponed a decision on whether the single currency coins should be multi-sided.

To help blind people tell one coin from another, an expert group had suggested making it seven-sided but vending machine operators have expressed concern about the effect of multi-sided coins on their business. -- Fredrik Dahl, Brussels newsroom +32 2 287 68 11
